methodological_rigor.justification: Population-based Swedish cohort of 778,943 women born 1985-1998 linking SVEVAC/NVR/PDR vaccination records to NPR/NCR outcomes with individual-level linkage via personal identity number. Vaccination treated as time-varying exposure with delayed entry and attained age as time scale; Poisson regression with natural-spline age term, calendar year, county, parental education/income, parental HPV history. Sensitivity analyses include 1- and 2-year buffer periods and site-stratified analyses. Residual confounding (smoking, sexual activity) is acknowledged and addressed via socioeconomic proxies. Statistical approach is appropriate; however, no formal multiplicity adjustment is reported across the multiple stratified IRRs, and potential detection-bias direction is noted only qualitatively.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Individual cohort study (Oxford 2b) with direct public-health relevance to vaccination policy. Findings (fully adjusted IRR 0.63 overall; 0.45 for vaccination at 10-16y; population-level reductions in subsidized/catch-up cohorts) support continued scale-up of publicly funded and school-based HPV vaccination at younger ages to prevent high-grade vulvovaginal lesions, extending cervical-cancer evidence to noncervical HPV-related outcomes.

reporting_quality.justification: Authors explicitly state adherence to STROBE. The Methods clearly describe data sources, eligibility, exposure, outcome ICD-10 codes (N901/N902/D071/C51 for vulva; N891/N892/D072/C52 for vagina), covariates, statistical models and sensitivity analyses; a flowchart (Figure 1) documents cohort assembly. Ethics approval/consent waiver is stated. Data availability is limited: the Swedish registers are not openly shareable and no code or analytic dataset link is provided in the excerpt, restricting reproducibility.

novelty_literature.justification: The work extends a known association (HPV vaccination reduces vulvovaginal precancers/cancers) previously reported in a Danish cohort (Dehlendorff 2021) and a trial systematic review, with the addition of Swedish nationwide data, a larger cohort, and explicit birth-cohort/program-level comparison. It is a meaningful incremental confirmation and quantification rather than a novel mechanism or method.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is concise, well structured and follows a JAMA-family question/findings/meaning format in the abstract. Tables and figures are clearly referenced and the time-varying exposure handling is explained in both text and figure legend. Limitations are thoroughly and specifically discussed. Prose is clear throughout.

key_strengths: Very large nationwide cohort (n=778,943) with individual-level register linkage and up to 17 years of follow-up
Rigorous time-varying exposure design with delayed entry, attained age as time scale, and buffer-period sensitivity analyses
Age-at-vaccination stratification (10-16y vs >=17y) showing stronger effect at younger ages (IRR 0.45, 95% CI 0.32-0.65)
Birth-cohort analysis aligned to opportunistic/subsidized/catch-up program structure, directly informing vaccination policy
STROBE-adherent reporting with explicit acknowledgement of bias directions (toward null) for key limitations
key_concerns: Observational design precludes causal inference; residual confounding from smoking and sexual behaviour cannot be excluded
Vaccination misclassification in SVEVAC (~8% anonymous records) and cervical-vs-vaginal lesion attribution challenges
No analytic code or dataset release; register data access is restricted, limiting reproducibility
Limited number of invasive vulvovaginal cancer cases; the study cannot assess cancer endpoint separately
Incremental novelty over the 2021 Danish cohort and prior trial meta-analysis; the main added value is scale and program-level analysis
chief_reviewer.rationale: A well-conducted nationwide cohort study with clear public-health implications for HPV vaccination policy; appropriate for a top-tier general-medicine/oncology venue (Tier 1) with minor revisions on code/data-sharing transparency.
